{{Short description|none}}
'''Mathematics and artificial intelligence''' (AI) have been interrelated since the initial development of [[AI]].
On one hand, [[mathematics]] plays a key role in artificial intelligence. For example, many AI algorithms use methods relying on [[Mathematical optimization|optimization]], [[statistics]] and [[linear algebra]]. On the other hand, researchers have for decades been trying to use AI and computers to help solve [[mathematics problem]]s.
The impact of AI has been pronounced in mathematics, where results are exactly verifiable.

== Background ==

=== Mathematics in AI ===
Many AI systems aim to approximate a set of data. This data, represented as numbers, is combined with weights using the techniques of [[linear algebra]]. The weighted data is typically non-linearized using for instance a [[sigmoid function]], before defining a [[loss function]] to minimize. The loss function is then minimized using an [[Mathematical optimization|optimization]] algorithm, for example [[gradient descent]]. This produces a set of weights which can be used to approximate the initial data.
[[File:Gradient descent maximum likelihood.svg|thumb|AI relies on mathematical techniques such as [[gradient descent]]]]

=== AI in mathematics ===
In mathematics the goal is often to [[Mathematical proof|prove]] a statement or theorem. Large language models ([[Large language model|LLM]]<nowiki/>s) can assist mathematicians by writing proofs or helping find mistakes in written work.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Tsoukalas |first1=George |title=Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search |date=2026-06-08 |eprint=2605.22763 |last2=Kovsharov |first2=Anton |last3=Shirobokov |first3=Sergey |last4=Surina |first4=Anja |last5=Firsching |first5=Moritz |last6=Bérczi |first6=Gergely |last7=Ruiz |first7=Francisco J. R. |last8=Suggala |first8=Arun |last9=Wagner |first9=Adam Zsolt |class=cs.AI }}</ref> LLMs can also be used to disprove theorems by finding counterexamples.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Tsoukalas |first1=George |title=Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search |date=2026-06-08 |eprint=2605.22763 |last2=Kovsharov |first2=Anton |last3=Shirobokov |first3=Sergey |last4=Surina |first4=Anja |last5=Firsching |first5=Moritz |last6=Bérczi |first6=Gergely |last7=Ruiz |first7=Francisco J. R. |last8=Suggala |first8=Arun |last9=Wagner |first9=Adam Zsolt |class=cs.AI }}</ref> Since mathematics is verifiable, once a proof is written it can be verified by checking that every line of the proof follows from the assumptions, for example by using a [[proof assistant]] such as [[Lean (proof assistant)|Lean]]. This makes mathematics very suitable as training data for AI.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mathematics and the formal turn |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/2024-61-02/S0273-0979-2024-01832-1/viewer/ |archive-url=http://web.archive.org/web/20251024154449/https://www.ams.org/journals/bull/2024-61-02/S0273-0979-2024-01832-1/viewer/ |archive-date=2025-10-24 |access-date=2026-08-19 |website=www.ams.org |language=en}}</ref>

== History ==
After the computer revolution, computers have made huge strides in mathematics, for example by helping to solve large numerical calculations in physics, engineering and military research. In 1956, a significant step was made when mathematicians built a program able to prove many of the theorems from [[Bertrand Russell|Russel]] and [[Alfred North Whitehead|Whitehead]]'s [[Principia Mathematica]]. The [[Logic Theorist]], as it became known, has been dubbed "the first artificial intelligence program".<ref name="mccCrevRussNorv">{{Harvnb|McCorduck|2004|pp=123–125}}, {{Harvnb|Crevier|1993|pp=44–46}} and {{Harvnb|Russell|Norvig|2021|p=17}}</ref>

During the 1960s, key strides were made in the theoretical foundations of artificial intelligence.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Nilsson |first=Nils J. |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/quest-for-artificial-intelligence/32C727961B24223BBB1B3511F44F343E |title=The Quest for Artificial Intelligence |date=2009 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-11639-8 |location=Cambridge}}</ref> A decade later, computers began to be used in [[computer-assisted proofs]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Celebrating the Four Color Theorem {{!}} College of Liberal Arts & Sciences {{!}} Illinois |url=https://las.illinois.edu/news/2017-10-18/celebrating-four-color-theorem |access-date=2026-08-16 |website=las.illinois.edu |language=en}}</ref> 

In 2017, [[Transformer (deep learning)|transformer]] architecture, a key component in modern LLMs, was developed using mathematics.<ref name="2017_Attention_Is_All_You_Need">{{cite conference |last1=Vaswani |first1=Ashish |author1-link=Ashish Vaswani |last2=Shazeer |first2=Noam |author2-link=Noam Shazeer |last3=Parmar |first3=Niki |last4=Uszkoreit |first4=Jakob |last5=Jones |first5=Llion |last6=Gomez |first6=Aidan N |author6-link=Aidan Gomez |last7=Kaiser |first7=Łukasz |last8=Polosukhin |first8=Illia |date=Dec 2017 |title=Attention is All you Need |url=https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2017/file/3f5ee243547dee91fbd053c1c4a845aa-Paper.pdf |series=Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems |publisher=Curran Associates, Inc. |volume=30 |arxiv=1706.03762 |editor=I. Guyon and U. Von Luxburg and S. Bengio and H. Wallach and R. Fergus and S. Vishwanathan and R. Garnett |book-title=[[Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems|31st Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS)]]}}</ref> In 2021, [[Google DeepMind|DeepMind]]'s AI enabled researchers to identify patterns in mathematics which had remained elusive to humans.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Castelvecchi |first=Davide |date=2021-12-01 |title=DeepMind's AI helps untangle the mathematics of knots |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-021-03593-1 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=600 |issue=7888 |pages=202 |doi=10.1038/d41586-021-03593-1 |pmid=34853424 |bibcode=2021Natur.600..202C }}</ref> Google then launched [[AlphaGeometry]] in 2024, which was able to use artificial intelligence to solve advanced problems in Euclidean geometry.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Roberts |first1=Siobhan |date=17 January 2024 |title=A.I.'s Latest Challenge: the Math Olympics |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/01/17/science/ai-computers-mathematics-olympiad.html |access-date=26 January 2024 |website=The New York Times}}</ref>

== Present ==
{{Main|List of mathematical discoveries by artificial intelligence}}

Up until roughly 2024, large language models (LLMs) were poor at doing mathematics.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Werner |first=John |title=AI Is Usually Bad At Math. Here's Why It Matters |url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/johnwerner/2024/10/07/ai-is-usually-bad-at-math-heres-what-will-happen-if-it-gets-better/ |access-date=2026-08-16 |website=Forbes |language=en}}</ref> Since then, LLMs from major companies have made significant strides in mathematics, heralding an "AI Revolution in Math".<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kakaes |first=Konstantin |date=2026-04-13 |title=The AI Revolution in Math Has Arrived |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-ai-revolution-in-math-has-arrived-20260413/ |access-date=2026-08-16 |website=Quanta Magazine |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kakaes |first=Konstantin |date=2026-08-03 |title=Why the Legendary Erdős Problems Are Falling to AI |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/why-the-legendary-erdos-problems-are-falling-to-ai-20260803/ |access-date=2026-08-16 |website=Quanta Magazine |language=en}}</ref> Some of the most significant breakthroughs are summarized in the following table.

In 2026 the [[First Proof]] [https://1stproof.org] project was launched to benchmark the capability of current AI models to perform research level mathematics.
[[File:FrontierMath Tier 4 (v2).png|thumb|Peak LLM performance on FrontierMath AI benchmark ]]

== Discussion ==
Concerns have been raised that the importance of the problems solved by AI in mathematics is overstated, and that the companies publishing these results are using the proofs as advertising for their models.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hart |first=Robert |date=2026-08-11 |title=The AI takeover of mathematics has begun |url=https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/977273/the-ai-takeover-of-mathematics-has-begun |access-date=2026-08-16 |website=The Verge |language=en-US}}</ref> There is also the question of attribution when AI makes a mathematical discovery.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Lee |first=Melissa |date=2026-08-09 |title=Generative AI has changed mathematics forever. Where to from here? |url=https://theconversation.com/generative-ai-has-changed-mathematics-forever-where-to-from-here-288954 |access-date=2026-08-16 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US}}</ref> Furthermore, the prohibitive price of the best AI models can potentially restrict mathematical research to elite institutions.<ref>{{Cite web |title='Brutal' math test stumps AI but not human experts |url=https://www.science.org/content/article/brutal-math-test-stumps-ai-not-human-experts |access-date=2026-08-16 |website=www.science.org |language=en}}</ref> To address some of these issues, several mathematicians have signed the Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics.

Mathematician [[Terence Tao]] has argued that AI will fundamentally change the way mathematics is done in the future.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2026-08-13 |title=Watch: Fields Medalist Terence Tao on Artificial Intelligence and Why We Do Math |url=https://www.simonsfoundation.org/2026/08/13/fields-medalist-terence-tao-on-artificial-intelligence-and-why-we-do-math/ |access-date=2026-08-16 |website=Simons Foundation |language=en-US}}</ref> In particular, AI will soon generate proofs that are verifiable by proof assistants yet indigestible to humans. The role of the mathematician will therefore have to involve greater emphasis on digesting and disseminating proofs.<ref>{{cite arXiv |last=Tao |first=Terence |title=Mathematics in the age of AI |date=2026-08-17 |class=math.HO |eprint=2608.16753}}</ref>
